summary: Space-Craft is a website designed to make the information provided by the SPHEREx telescope more accessible and user-friendly for teenagers and anyone interested in astronomy. It provides GIFs that illustrate the evolution of selected or searched celestial objects over time.
details:
Space-Craft is a web app that lets anyone see how a patch of sky changes over time using real data from NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope, which has been mapping the whole sky every six months since May 2025. It has two parts:

  1. Sky map. A flat map of the sky shows 20 curated objects, such as Andromeda, the Crab Nebula, Barnard’s Star, and a brown dwarf called WISE 0855. It also shows the Milky Way band and the ecliptic (the Sun’s path). Clicking an object opens a card that explains what it is, how far away it is, and what to look for. Twelve objects have GIFs made from real SPHEREx images. The others have illustrative animations.
  2. Explore the sky. Users type an object name or RA/Dec coordinates. The server finds SPHEREx images in NASA’s IRSA archive, downloads a small cutout of each one, aligns them, and returns an animated GIF. Moving objects like asteroids and comets can be added through their JPL Horizons ID, and a “difference mode” subtracts the fixed stars so only things that move or change brightness stand out.

Results are cached, so a repeated request returns instantly. The interface also has a collapsible guide and a Spanish/English toggle.

What benefits does it have?

  • It turns complex astronomical data into something a non-expert can use without installing software or knowing how to query a scientific archive.
  • It teaches how astronomers find moving and changing objects, the same principle used to discover Pluto.
  • It is free to use and works on phones and computers.
  • It is bilingual, which makes it more accessible.
  • Pages can be shared through direct links (for example ?nombre=Barnard%27s%20Star) or embedded in other sites with an iframe, so teachers can use it in class.

What is the intended impact?
We want to make real NASA science easier for students, teachers, and curious people to explore. The goal is to turn “looking at the sky” into an active investigation: spot what moves, compare dates, and build intuition about stars, nebulae, and galaxies, instead of just reading about them.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Front end: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a single page, with the HTML canvas for the map and the pixel-art animations. No external frameworks.
  • Back end: Python with FastAPI and Uvicorn. Background worker threads handle the GIF requests.
  • Astronomy libraries: Astropy, Astroquery, and Reproject, plus SPHEREx image data from NASA/IPAC IRSA, SIMBAD for name lookups, and JPL Horizons for moving objects.
  • Deployment: Docker, with the server hosted on Render’s free tier. The static page can also be hosted separately, for example on Vercel, Netlify, or GitHub Pages.
  • Development and testing: Colab-style scripts for the image processing, and a headless browser for testing the interface.
  • Hardware: No special hardware is needed. It runs on a standard laptop and on a small cloud server (512 MB RAM).

How is your project creative?

  • It uses a Minecraft-inspired pixel-art look, with blocky icons, colors, and a grass-block logo, to make a serious astronomy topic feel friendly and game-like.
  • Each object type has its own icon and color, and labels are positioned automatically with connector lines so they don’t overlap.
  • Where real data isn’t available, it uses clearly labeled illustrative animations (a moving star, a pulsing variable star, a flaring red dwarf), so every object still teaches something.
  • It turns raw telescope data into short animations anyone can understand.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility: plain-language explanations, a built-in glossary and guide, and a bilingual interface for people without a science background.
  • Scientific honesty: real data and illustrative animations are labeled differently, and the page says the illustrative motions are exaggerated.
  • Performance and cost: NASA downloads can be slow, so we limit the field size, number of images, and simultaneous requests. We also cache results and designed the app to run on a free server with limited memory.
  • Respect for NASA’s servers: the limits and caching also keep us from overloading IRSA.
  • Reliability: we chose a long-running server instead of serverless hosting, because generating a GIF takes several minutes and needs heavy libraries.
  • Ease of use and sharing: responsive design, shareable links, and an embeddable page.
